subject: Biology
title: Plants and Soil
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Plants and Soil.

hook.text: Soil is not just dirt. It's a living community of minerals, microbes, fungi, and water.

buildup.text: Plants absorb nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium from soil—the three key nutrients for growth.

discovery.text: Mycorrhizal fungi extend root networks by a hundred times, trading minerals for plant sugars.

twist.text: Industrial farming depletes soil. A third of the world's topsoil is degraded.

climax.text: Healthy soil stores carbon, filters water, and supports food production for 8 billion people.

punchline.text: Take care of the soil. Everything grows from it.

quiz.question: What do mycorrhizal fungi trade with plant roots?

details.summary: Soil provides plants with water, mineral nutrients, physical support, and hosts the microbial partners essential for nutrient uptake. Soil composition, pH, organic matter content, and microbial community directly determine which plants can grow and how productively they perform.
details.whyItMatters: Healthy soil is the foundation of agriculture and natural ecosystems. Soil degradation from erosion, compaction, and chemical depletion threatens global food security, with an estimated one-third of agricultural soils already degraded worldwide.
takeaways: Plants obtain 13 essential mineral nutrients from soil through root absorption
Soil pH determines nutrient availability and which plants can thrive
Approximately one-third of global agricultural soils are degraded

faq.question: Why does soil pH matter so much for plant growth?
faq.answer: pH controls the solubility of essential nutrients. Iron and manganese become unavailable at high pH. Phosphorus is most available near neutral pH. Aluminum becomes toxic at low pH. Each plant species has an optimal pH range where all nutrients are accessible.

faq.question: How do plants get nitrogen from soil?
faq.answer: Most plants absorb nitrate or ammonium from soil solution through root hairs. Legumes form partnerships with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules that convert atmospheric N2 directly. Mycorrhizal fungi also help many plants access nitrogen from organic matter.
